declared.title: How do income changes impact on mental health and wellbeing for working-age adults? A systematic review and meta-analysis
declared.foundIn: counter-evidence report reports/money-happiness/counter-evidence.md; OpenAlex search « how do income changes impact on mental health and wellbeing working-age adults systematic review meta-analysis » (2026-11-22)

population: adults aged 16-64; 136 studies (12.5% RCTs), 86 meta-analysed; English-language studies, countries not listed in the abstract

findings.text: An income rise that lifts people out of poverty goes with better mental health

support.sentence: A binary income increase lifting individuals out of poverty was associated with 0·13 SD improvement in mental health measures (95% CI 0·07 to 0·20; n=42 128; 18 studies), considerably larger than other income increases (0·01 SD improvement, 0·002 to 0·019; n=216 509, 14 studies).

findings.text: Other income rises, not out of poverty, go with almost no change in mental health

support.sentence: A binary income increase lifting individuals out of poverty was associated with 0·13 SD improvement in mental health measures (95% CI 0·07 to 0·20; n=42 128; 18 studies), considerably larger than other income increases (0·01 SD improvement, 0·002 to 0·019; n=216 509, 14 studies).

findings.text: Leaving poverty goes with the largest gain in wellbeing

support.sentence: For wellbeing, increases out of poverty were associated with 0·38 SD improvement (0·09 to 0·66; n=101 350, 8 studies) versus 0·16 for other income increases (0·07 to 0·25; n=62 619, 11 studies).

findings.text: Other income rises still go with better wellbeing, by a smaller amount

support.sentence: For wellbeing, increases out of poverty were associated with 0·38 SD improvement (0·09 to 0·66; n=101 350, 8 studies) versus 0·16 for other income increases (0·07 to 0·25; n=62 619, 11 studies).

findings.text: The authors rate the certainty of this evidence low or very low (GRADE)

support.sentence: GRADE certainty was low or very low.

limits: the authors' own GRADE: low or very low certainty; risk of bias high (30.1% of studies critical, 47.1% serious or high)
heterogeneity high (I2 = 79-87%); effects larger in low- and middle-income settings and in higher risk-of-bias studies
mostly non-randomised studies (12.5% RCTs): pooled estimates are associations, not clean causal effects
« other income increases » is not « once basic needs are met »: an indirect test of the book's threshold
English-language studies only; countries not listed in the abstract (full text not read)
